No part of this pub- lication may be reproduced, stored in a retrieval system, or trans- mitted, in any form or by any means, electronic, mechanical. photocopying, recording, or otherwise, without the prior written permission of the publisher. LORETTA LYNN -Loretta, MCA MCA3217. Produced by Owen Bradley. A solid set of songs places the emphasis on Lynn's upfront voice. The pace varies from slow ballads such as "It's Too Late To Love Me Now" to the spicy love song "Naked In The Rain." Piano, drums, guitar, bass, electric bass and strings back up Lynn in the uncluttered Bradley produc- tion. The LP should benefit from the promotional efforts sur- rounding the new Lynn autobiographical movie "Coal Miner's Daughter." Best cuts' "Sweet, Sweet Daddy," "It's Too Late To Love Me Now," "You're A Cross I Can't Bear," "I've Been Lonely So Long," "I Should Be Over You By Now." ORIGINAL MOTION PICTURE SOUNDTRACK -Coal Miner's Daughter, MCA MCA5107. Produced by Owen Bradley. Sounding remarkably like Loretta Lynn, actress Sissy Spacek handles the material on this soundtrack incredibly well. From "There He Goes" (which could be the first Spacek single) to "Coal Miner's Daughter" which ends the soundtrack and the film, one feels that Lynn is handling the vocals. Included in the soundtrack is Levan Helm's version of "Blue Moon Of Kentucky," and several selections by Beverly D'Angelo who plays Patsy Cline in the film, performing "Walking After Mid- night," "Crazy," "Sweet Dreams" and duets Spacek on "Back In Baby's Arms." One of the better film soundtracks recently, the material is treated with care and perfection by producer Bradley. Best cuts: "There He Goes," "I'm A Hanky Tank Girl," "I Fall To Pieces," "Blue Moon Of Kentucky," "Back In Baby's Arms," and "Coal Miner's Daughter." REX ALLEN JR.- Oklahoma Rose, Warner Bros. BSK3403. Produced by Rex Allen Jr., Norro Wilson. "Oklahoma Rose," a fascinating full -length story told in song, is an outstanding musical effort that also happens to be one of country's first "concept" albums. Using his own band and top Nashville players, and cowriting a lot of the material himself, Allen creates a unique and thoroughly enjoyable LP that seems to grow better with each listening. "Oklahoma Rose" tells the saga of a small town girl who abandons boyfriend and home to follow the bright lights of Hollywood. Though collectively the songs relate the events and emotions of the two main characters, each song stands individually on its own as a po- tential single, and Allen sounds better than ever. Best cuts: "Prairie Moon," "It's Over," "Hollywood," "You're Gonna Be A Star," "Yippi Cry Yi." DEBBY BOONE -Love Has No Reason, Warner /Curb BSK3419. Produced by Larry Butler. The material, production and arrangements all work quite effectively on this, perhaps Debby's strongest album todate. Taking a country twist, pro- ducer Butler has selected a wide ranging assortment of songs which Boone glides through. With her vocals out front, Boone works effortlessly on Diane Pfieffer's "Just When I Needed A Love Song," and Kenny O'Dell's "When It's Just You And Me." Nashville's top players, the album is the first of hope- fully a series of Butler and Boone combinations. Best cuts: Those mentioned above plus "Are You On The Road To Lavin' Me Again," "Love Put A Song In My Heart." tt First Time Around THE TASMANIAN DEVILS -Warner Bros. BSK3400. Pro- duced by Erik Jacobsen, the Tazmanian Devils. San Francisco Bay quintet plays an infectious brand of spare pop -rock. The sound is reminiscent of Talking Heads in its leanness, the subject matter and vocal phrasing are far more in keeping with conventional pop sensibilities. "Sender To Me" and "Don't Slip" have subtle reggae undertones while "Music" is a nice slice of blue -eyed funk. However, the standout track is the hypnotic "Spy In The House Of Love" which is soft yet commanding. Lead vocals by Pat Craig and Dennis Hogan fit the format well. Best cuts: "Spy In The House Of Love," "Sender To Me," "Music," "Don't Slip," "My Obsession." PRIVATE LIGHTNING -A &M SP4791. Produced by Robin Geoffrey Cable. This sextet delivers mainstream, commercial rock that possesses plenty of hooks and enough lyrical clout to appeal to the AOR audience. The music is tight, shying away from the overblown delivery some of the older bands seem to prefer. Several cuts are well worth hearing and the addition of Patty Van Ness on violin is a real visual treat. Band has a solid reputation throughout New England and should break there first. Best cuts: "Physical Speed," "Bright City," "Song Of The Kite." BRYAN ADAMS -A &M SP4800. Produced by Jim Valiance, Bryan Adams. A nice approach to basic pop /rock is evidenced here, although composer /pianist /vocalist /guitarist Adams displays a penchant for hard rock that works. A Canadian, he had a disco hit last year that belies his rock roots. These nine cuts show promise, although the lyrics aren't as biting as the market demands. There are some tunes that stand out, though, and the music rocks out with gusto. Best cuts: "Hiding From Love," "State Of Mind," "Win Some, Lose Some." Spotlight , BILLY JOEL -Glass Houses, Columbia FC36384. Pro- duced by Phil Ramone. Released on the heels of Joel's best album Grammy for "52nd Street," the singer /song- writer rocks out more than on previous albums. The ma- terial is more biting and harder edged, punctuated by the effervescent playing of Joel's band. Joel's writing still leans towards the mainstream with plenty of hooks and memorable melodies, although he leans more towards the progressive (at least for him) on several cuts. His vo- cals also take on different tones, sounding very similar to Paul McCartney on "Don't Ask Me Why" and then changes gears to sound more in line with contemporary new wave singers. While there aren't as many slick and sweet ballads as on "52nd Street" and "The Stranger," it is to Joel's benefit that he has altered his successful style and dared to try something out of the norm. There's even one tune in which Joel dazzles with French verse. Superb guitar and sax work cushion Joel's piano. Best cuts: "You May Be Right," "Don't Ask Me Why," "Sometimes A Fantasy," "I Don't Want To Be Alone." eCla ssiccal C WENDY CARLOS- Switched -On Brandenburgs- CBS M2X35895. Carlos' survey of the six Bach "Brandenburg" Concertos began in 1968 with the landmark "Switched On Bach" album, and about half of this double -LP set has ap- peared in previous releases. Dealers can point to some minor changes in earlier interpretations, the remastered sound and the special two -disk pricing as incentives for customers now to acquire the collection in its entirety. Also the "crossover" market is a potent force. Even those who perform on conven- tional instruments -let alone other synthesists -must admire the singing quality and rhythmic bouyancy that Carlos achieves with her banks of electronic gear. Billboard's Recommended LPs Pop DARYL HALL -Sacred Songs, RCA AFL13375. Produced by Robert Fripp. This is the Fripp-produced Hall LP that has been delayed two years because of contractual and legal diffi- culties. Now it is here, and it was well worth the wait, as Hall's soul influenced vocals find their perfect foil in Fripp's "Frippertronics." The result is space fink that works very well, its head very much in the clouds while its heart and soul re- main solidly on the ground. Best cuts: "Babs And Babs," "NYCNY," "Survive," "Without Tears." JOHN MILES -Sympathy, Arista AB4261. Produced by Alan Parsons, Gary Lyons. An artist with the potential to break big in the mainstream progressive rock market is John Miles, whose latest release, "Sympathy," is a solid effort anchored by mature songwriting and to the mark instrumentation and arrangements. Miles has a good high rock voice, which he can bring down for effect and which serves him very well here. Best cuts: "Sympathy," "We All Fall Down," "C'Est La Vie," "Can't Keep A Good Man Down." STONEBOLT -Keep It Alive, RCA KKL10357. Produced by Walter Stewart, Ray Roper. Stonebolt has all the ingredients to achieve Top 40 airplay: commercial hooks, strong vocals and hummable melodies. The playing is cohesive and with more of an identity, this quintet could make a decent show- ing. Best cuts: "Price Of Love," "Love Struck," "Don't Ya Hide lt." GENTLE GIANT -Civilian, Columbia JC36341. Produced by Onward U.S. Productions. Gentle Giant debuts on CBS with the kind of engaging progressive rock it made while on Capi- tol. The songs here are shorter, punchier and more adaptable for AOR radio. The band's lyrics are particularly interesting and the playing is clean and precise. Best cuts: "Conven- ience," "Underground," "Inside Out," "All Through The Night." TRIUMPH - Progressions Of Power, RCA AFL13524. Produced by Triumph. Canadian power rock trio turns in a set of energetic rockers that not only showcases fine guitar work but also a sense of melody. While the group is not among the most original, it does have an audience that appreciates this kind of music. Best cuts: "I Can Survive," "I Live For The Weekend," "Woman In Love," "Hard Road." THE DUDEK, FINNIGAN, KRUEGER BAND, Columbia JC35770. Produced by James Newton Howard, Andy Johns. The music of Les Dudek, Mike Finnigan and Jim Krueger, unlike most sidemen turned frontmen, is not just technically precise. The eight tunes here are solid pop -rock pieces with r &b and jazz undertones in places. Dudek's rousing guitar work is kept in the context of hook -filled songs so the playing never becomes excessive or showy. Finnigan's heartfelt vocals shine and Krueger's guitar playing is crisp. Best cuts: "It's All About You," "Drinkin' Alone," "You Cut So Deep," "Angels Fall," "Just Be Happy " URBAN VERBS -Warner Bros. BSK3418. Produced by Mike Thorne. From Washington, D.C., this group sounds urban with J its raw, slashing music. At times, the group brings to mind the best of the Doors' moody and somewhat i h Y d sc ordant ma- terial. This is especially true of the understated "Luca Brasi" and "Good Life," yet another attack on the lifestyle of Califor- nians. This LP proves experimental punk music did not die in 1977. Best cuts: "Good Life," "Ring -Ring (My Telephone's Talking)," "Subways," "Luca Brasi." PUBLIC IMAGE LTD,- Second Edition, Island 2WX3288. No producer listed. For specialized tastes, this two record set is John "Rotten" Lydon's post -Sex Pistols experiment. He still possesses a buzzsaw of a voice though now the musical back- ing has changed. As with the avant -garde James White And The Blacks, Public Image uses a steady disco backbeat much of the time. However, Lydon's ranting voice and odd melodies put this on the extreme edge of the mainstream. Danceable "Bad Baby" is the most accessible cut. Best cuts: "Bad Baby," "No Birds," "Albatross," "Swan Lake." BRUFORD - Polydor PD16261. Produced by Ron Malo, Bill Bruford. Bill Bruford, for which this quartet is named, has been a percussionist for many top progressive rock bands over the years including Yes and King Crimson. However, this arresting eight -song set is mostly jazz in the Weather Report vein. The band reaches its peak on such steamy instrumen- tals as "Land's End," "Q.E.D.," "Joe Frazier" and the quiet "Palewell Park." The pop "Plans For 1.D.," with its sly hook and harmonies, is the only concession to mainstream pop val- ues. Most cuts fit into AOR and jazz formats. Best cuts: Those mentioned. ROADMASTER- Fortress, Mercury SRM13814. Produced by Flo & Eddie with John Stronach. Second Mercury album from these Midwestern rockers showcases the quintet's hard -driv- ing but melodic style. Solid guitars and drums are at the mu- sic's core, while Mac McNally fronts the lineup with expres- sive and confident vocals. Best cuts: "Ride The Wind Away," "Too Long, Too Long," "Satisfied Woman." MIKE RUTHERFORD- Smallcreep's Day, Passport PB9843 (JEM). No producer listed. Genesis bassist Rutherford debuts with his first solo album that is a concept (side two) about a man who works on an assembly line for 40 years without knowing what his contribution to the final project is. The al- bum is on the progressive side of the spectrum but suitable for AOR formats. Best cuts: "Moonshine," "Time And Time Again." "Cats And Rats." MARTI WEBB -Tell Me On A Sunday, Polydor PD16260. Pro- duced by Andrew Lloyd Webber. This is the latest of Webber's concept albums, recalling his work on "Evita" and "Jesus Christ, Superstar." Webb's is an appealing yet sophisticated vocal style, which works well whatever the musical setting: bold and Spectoresque as in the current U.K. hit, "Take That Look Off Your Face," or subtle and somber as in the album's title cut. Musicians like Rod Argent and Jon Hiseman lend the project extra weight. Best cuts: Those cited, plus "It's Not The End Of The World." BROADWAY CAST ALBUM -Oklahoma, RCA CBL13572. Pro- duced for records by Thomas Z. Shepard. Thirty five years old and the score to this Broadway revival sounds as young and wonderful as the cast, led by Laurence Guittard and Christine Andreas. Show music fans will appreciate the three songs never released with the Decca original caster including the remarkable Rodgers & Hammerstein character song, "Lonely Room." Best cuts: All. IN CROWD -Man From New Guinea, Mango MLPS9577 (Is- land). Produced by Phil Mathias. "Reggae Groove" is an in- strumental dance number that is more pure soul than reggae and is somewhat reminiscent of Kool & the Gang's "Ladies Night." The rest of the side is lilting, infectious reggae which has a soft almost adult contemporary feel. The crystal clear harmonic arrangements of the voices are closer to the Mills Brothers than Bob Marley. Best cuts: All of side two. soul PEGGY BLUE -I Got Love, MCA MCA3223. Produced by Jerry Ragovoy. Blue has sung backup for Norman Connors, Esther Phillips, Staple Singers, Stephanie Mills and others. On her solo debut, she sings seven songs written or cowritten by pro- ducer Ragovoy and Marvin Gaye's "Dancing In The Streets." Each track gets a sensitive reading and evokes different moods. A few cuts are very danceable although Blue's voice is more suitable for relaxing listening. Strings and horns ar- rangements add a nice touch. Best cuts: "When You Got A Good Groove Goin'," "It's The End," "I Got Love." jazz BILL O'CONNELL- Searching, Inner City IC1035. Produced by Eddie Oberste. Pianist O'Connell plays his jazz in a Bill Evans vein, but he exhibits a lot of originality here in six origi- nal compositions, four of them his own. Accompanied by Mike Willens on bass and Jeff Papez on drums, O'Connell has turned out an album that has unflagging appeal and warmth. Best cuts: "White Light," "Four A.M." RAY WILKES -Dark Blue Man, Inner City IC1051. Produced by Gene Elders, Ray Wilkes. This is a beautifully conceived and executed album that ranges from classical guitar solos by Wilkes to ambitious arrangements with strings and saxes. Along the way David Ferguson plays some tasteful piano, but there's no question that Wilkes is the star of this jazz outing. Best cuts: All. BOBBY KNIGHT'S GREAT AMERICAN TROMBONE CO. -Cream Of The Crop, Pye N5003. Produced by Bobby Knight, Marty Morgan. A spectacular program of 10 tunes with six trom- bones spotted in front of a splendid three -man rhythm sec- tion. Knight's 'bone is joined by Carl Fontana, Phil Teele, Lew McCreary, Charlie Loper and the late Frank Rosolino in a dar- ing and exceptionally musical experiment which comes off as bright, swinging and (at times) humorous tour de force. Best cuts: "I Got Rhythm," "When I Fall In Love," "Li'l Bit." HELIOCENTRIC -Discovery DS806. Produced by Heliocentric. Quartet makes an auspicious bow with a program which blends various meters with Latin underpinnings and an ad- ventureous, crystal attack. Horns and keyboards are the basic melody instruments with drums and bass cleanly aggressive. The modern jazz is infectious and free flowing, albeit well or- ganized. Group will need some promotion to spin it out from all the new bands emerging. Best cuts: "Afferent Connec- tion," "Arrow," "Cloud Mountain." RUSSELL GARCIA- Variations For Flugelhorn, String Quartet, Bass & Drums, Trend TR522. Produced by Albert Marx. This is heady stuff, an intense listening experience in which Chuck Findley's mellow flugelhorn is counterpoised against a string quartet with bass and drums kicking the interventions along. There is a quasi -classical feel to Garcia's compositions but the jazz emphasis overwhelms. This is the label's second digi- tal effort with Sony equipment and the sound is indeed crisp. Garcia's recent absence from disks has now been counter- acted by this fine work. Best cuts: "Alchemy," "Swing Lightly," "Lament." BOB FLORENCE -Big Band Live At Concerts By The Sea, Trend TR523. Produced by Albert Marx. L.A. area band makes a roaring debut on this debut digital disk for tiny L.A. label. Florence's six tunes are well fashioned showcase the many colors of the brass and reed section. While it plays with con- viction, the band lacks a distinct signature but the music is engaging and rich and mellow and bombastic so that the Sony digital taping offers greater instrumental presence. Best cuts: "Lonely Carousel," "I'll Remember," "Party Hearty." DALLAS JAll ORCHESTRA -Super Chicken, DJO unnum- bered. Produced by Galen Jeter. These Lone Star state pro- fessionals have popped with a laudable package comprising two 12 -inch LPs comprising 12 tunes. With five trumpets and four trombones, it's a powerful ensemble with the ability to purvey fat ballad sounds with a number of uptempo jumpers. Best cuts: "The More I See You," "Nothing Grows In The Shade." Record World To Open 3 New Stores NEW YORK -The Record World retail chain will have three addi- tional outlets by June, according to Roy Imber, who operates the TSS/ Record World locations out of Elroy Enterprises of Freeport, N.Y. In April, Record World will have a 4,500 square feet unit in Peekskill, N.Y. at Alexander's Mall on Route 6; a 2,000 square feet unit will open in May at the Sears Shopping Center in Commack, N.Y.; and a 2,500 square feet outlet in Greenvale, N.Y., in the Wheatley Hills Plaza. 12 Videotape Lawsuit Continued from page 1 The complaint charges Video Shack. Inc.. a New York videotape dealer. with selling videotapes con- taining unauthorized material man- ufactured by Video Communi- cations. Inc.. -Video Tape Network and Media Home Entertainment. In addition. a number of' "John Does" arc listed as defendants. Video Communications is alleged to have failed to obtain proper li- censing from Northern Songs for its videotapes of "Welcome To Pepper - land." The Beatles Show. Parts 1 And 2" and The Beatles At Shea Stadium." Video Tape Network is similarly charged with its releases of "History Of The Beatles." and "Rock Gar- den." while Media Home Entertain- ment's alleged infringements in- volve "The Beatles Live In Tokyo." "Beatles Live At Shea Stadium." "Magical Mystery Tour" and "Around The Beatles." The complaint further charges that the defendants operate in "der- rogation" of Northern licensing agreements with third parties -none of whom are the defendants -which constitute unfair competition and unfair trade practices against the plaintiff to its "substantial and ir- reparable harm." The licensing agreements. the complaint declares. involve various licensees for dra- matic- musical rights. film rights and sound recording rights to many of the compositions used by the de- fendants in the videotapes. Northern is seeking punitive dam- ages from each defendant of $1 mil- lion in addition to copyright in- fringement damages of not less than $250 per infringement. The defendants also are called upon to place on notice all retail out- lets selling the videotapes to return them to the defendants. the defend- ants be required to turn over during the pendency of this action all copies of the tapes in their possession or un- der their control, and to turn over for destruction all allegedly infringing tapes. plates, molds. masters. nega- tives and other matter. Mobile Fidelity Into Jazz And Classical By ALAN PENCHANSKY CHICAGO - Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs has begun extending its reach into new repertoire areas. The diversification brings to the audio- phile label new jazz and classical series. slated for introduction in May. First classical releases. under EMI license. include Tchaikovsky's "1812 Overture" and "Romeo And Juliet." and Orffs "Carmina Burana." both conducted by Andre Provin. Jazz releases are Don Sebesky's "Three Works For Jazz Soloists And Orchestra." and "Le Jazz Grand." Michel Legrande, both from Gry- phon. and A &M Horizon's "Light On Light." by Seawind. Another new development at Mo- bile Fidelity is the appointment of Herb Belkin. former ABC Records and Motown executive, as president. And the L.A. -based label's pop /rock product flow is being increased in volume. Mobile Fidelity was the first label to popularize the half -speed master- ing technique in processing of li- censed material for audiophile re- lease. It's expected that company founder Brad Miller will concen- trate on ongoing technical work fol- lowing the executive restructuring. taking a reduced part in day to day label affairs. Miller is named com- pany chairman with Belkin's ap- pointment. The company's $15.98 list import pressings, among time leading sellers in the audiophile disk held. are mar- keted primarily through hi fi stores. Miller and partner Gary Giorgi first began licensing hit product for hi fi market exploitation in 1978. Jazz and classical titles will be is- sued two or three times annually. ac- cording to Belkin. who says the com- pany feels an obligation to give representation to these forms. How- ever. levels of expectation of sales success are somewhat lower. he notes. Release of pop /rock titles is more frequent. March will bring Styx' "Grand Illusion." Neil Diamond's "Hot August Night." Earl Klugh's "Fingerpainting" and "All Around My. Hat," by Steeleye Spann. This will he the single biggest release from the company. Despite the broadening musical emphasis. Belkin does not plan to tamper with the hi fi- directed mar- keting plan. "We're not interested in making hi fi shops into record stores or in being a total record company with a big catalog." he relates. The label places a production ceil- ing of 200.000 copies on each title and there is limitation of catalog size through a policy of regular dele- tions. Radio Programming LISTENERS' CHOICE -WHN -AM New York general manager Nick Verbitsky, left, presents Dolly Parton with awards as winner in the female vocalist an- nual WHN Listeners' Choice Awards. The presentation was made at the Re- sorts International Hotel in Atlantic City where the country singer was ap- pearing. KBPI -FM Leading Denver's A.M. Drive By DICK DENVER -Strong personalities teamed with an AOR format moved KBPI -FM ahead in the important morning drive segment in the fall Arbitron report. Program manager Frank Cody, who joined the station in spring of last year, credits the shift of Alan Baxter and Don Hawkins from KAZY -FM to KBPI in the late sum- mer for the gain in mornings. "They have been carrying the sta- tion," Cody says of his morning team. Cindy Elrod, operations man- ager, also points to Pete MacKay, who follows Baxter and Hawkins in a midday slot and also runs an oldies show on Sunday mornings. While Baxter and Hawkins moved the station from a 3.2 to a 3.6 share in morning drive, MacKay raised the midday share from 3.6 to 4.5. Overall, the station moved from 4.6 to 4.9. "I think in the '80s we're headed toward the personality," Cody says and mentions Chicago's Steve Dahl as an example. He said Baxter and Hawkins "sound very appropriate for what we want to do." He wants the station to become a personality rock station. Other things that have boosted the ratings of the station is that it took a survey of Denver area musical tastes when Cody came on board. "The most logical thing, since we have been known as an AOR sta- tion, was to go after the 18 -34 year - old- market," he states. When asked what the survey showed, Cody notes that the old standbys: the Beatles, Rolling Stones and Led Zeppelin are still popular; while artists like Rod Stew- art are "burn outs" and Cody cites Stewart's disco sounding "Do You Think I'm Sexy" as the main reason. Another reason for the fall book increase may be that about 11/2 years ago, according to Cody's estimate, the station was bought by the Sand- usky newspaper group. He says that before the sale, while the station was uncertain about its KELLEHER future, the "station was slowed down." He says there was little ad- vertising or promotion until after the sale. There still seems to be little ad- vertising, leading the cause of the in- crease back to the team of Baxter and Hawkins. In their morning show, Baxter or Hawkins will receive satirical calls from people who sound like Groucho Marx, an old man, or simi- lar putons, usually claiming to be a relative of one of the team. Another high point is a compre- hensive capsulization of the day's news and a weatherman known as Weatherman Bowman who goes into things such as explanations of jet streams which are causing cold air to pour into the area. Cody also admits that during his study of the market be found "people listen to a various number of different stations instead of hav- ing one allegiance" and that he real- izes he can't have all the audience all the time. He thinks that because of this, the station needs to "have a high regard for the listener" and it seems to be paying off. MIAMI AM STATION SWAPS FORMATS WMBM Into `Gold Soul 15' MIAMI -A format change on WMBM -AM here to what is being billed as "Gold Soul 15" is one more indication that what might be de- scribed as black MOR is a coming format for the 1980s. New program director Robert Hall has installed a format with similarities to KMJQ -FM Dallas, which is about to be syndicated by TM Programming (Billboard, March 15, 1980) and a new format just begun on WHAT -AM in Phila- delphia. WMBM has been into disco and a mass appeal black format, but Hall is now shooting for an audience 35 to 45 years old; the black business professional, man or woman. "The one with the money." Hall says with a grin. Hall says it was a mistake for his station to try to reach a general mar- ket mass audience. "We couldn't compete with WQAM -AM, WMJX (96 -X) and WHYI -FM (Y -100). In seeking a format, I decided to take the station back to where it came from, back to its roots." Explains Hall: "Now we're geared strictly to a black audience, al- though, because of the jazz we play, we are getting some white listeners." Programming is based on a series of color codes or flow clocks with blue, green, yellow and red lettered beads. The DJ reads the rings playing a red themed song, for instance when he comes to a red bead. The DJ may pick any one of 15 or 20 tunes from the color and letter -coded tapes cor- responding to the color and letter codes. There are six flow clocks for each different time of day. These dictate the form of music to be played -ro- mantic ballad, jazz, blues, r &b or current hit. "Sounds complicated, but it really isn't," Hall explains. "I don't pick the tunes, the DJ does. All I do is set the type of music to be played in the various time slot which gives the sta- tion a flowing feel. "We go the whole nine yards in artists, playing Ray Charles, Johnny Mathis, Sarah Vaughan, Ella Fitz- gerald, Bobby Blue Bland, B.B. King, Aretha Franklin, Jerry Butler, the old Temptations, Otis Redding, Diana Ross and the Supremes, Mar- tha Reeves and the Vandellas. The list is endless. The only music we don't play is disco and bubblegum." Local news is broadcast every hour on the hour for five minutes. Part of WMBM's appeal to the com- munity is that it is extremely com- munity- oriented. By SARA LANE During the day movie reviews, lo- cal gossip, wake -up body exercises, household tips, recipes, what's going on around town and other tidbits of information are offered by the disk jockeys. "We're certainly not a talk station, we're pure music and these bits and pieces of information last only about 25 seconds each." Hall explains. WMBM -AM disk jockeys are Ab- dul from 6:30 to IO a.m.; Connie Clare, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.; Stonewall Jackson, 3 to 7 p.m.; Vaughn Valen- tino 7 p.m. to midnight; and Hughie Ferguson midnight to 6:30 a.m. $67 Million Bid For 10 Stations Declined NEW YORK -There may not seem to be anything analogous be- tween baseball and radio, but just as ball players are traded in the spring, this spring is shaping up as a prime time to trade, buy and sell stations. Ed Coss - man. vice president of SJR, report- edly now wants $75 million for the package. Gabbert put the station on the air in 1957 and has operated three other stations, another in San Francisco and two in Honolulu, which he is also selling. He's getting out of radio and into television and is buying a UHF station in San Francisco. Eller, the former president of Combined Communications, is ex- pected to build another radio group. He did this when he headed Com- bined and then sold that group to Gannett Co. Possibly the most unusual trade is that put together by Metromedia. The company sold KNEW -AM San Francisco to Malrite Broadcasting for $5 million and then turned around and bought KJR -AM Seattle from Kaye -Smith Enter- prises for $ 10 million. Both KNEW and KJR are 5 kw stations with directional patterns at night. KJR is third in its market with a 6.0 share in the October /Novem- ber Arbitron while KNEW is 13th in its market with a 2.6 share. Possibly the best deal was achieved by country singer Charley Pride and forme TM Productions and Programming president Jim Long. They. through their Long - Pride Broadcasting Co., purchased KFOG -FM San Francisco from General Electric for $3.5 million, a figure some observers called "a steal." KFOG, which runs the Schulke beautiful music format. enjoys a 3.4 share while contemporary KIOI. which commanded almost three times as much money, had a 3.3 in the fall Arbitron. NIGHT OWL KMET -FM's Jim Ladd Rocks Station To Enviable Ratings LOS ANGELES -To thousands of Southern California rock listen- ers, Jim Ladd is more than just an- other nighttime 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. air personality. His mix of his some- times controversial "raps" with straightforward rock has made him one of the favorites at highly rated AOR KMET -FM. The night Arbi- tron shares for the station are its highest. "I almost got fired from KLOS- FM every day that I worked there," starts Ladd. "They were always call- ing me in and I was conservative there compared to what I am now." Ladd has been doing his mixture of talk and free form programming By CARY DARLING music ever since first entering radio 10 years ago at AOR KNAC -FM Long Beach, Calif. From there, he moved to AOR KLOS, where he stayed four years. The topics and the talk are spon- taneous. "I did a huge piece on the draft the other night and that was to- tally off top of my head. I take my ideas from the street," he says. "Dur- ing the night of the draft talk, listen- ers were calling up and giving me great songs to play which related to the theme." The music plays an integral part of the set. "Like when I was playing records about the draft, I wasn't fol- lowing Crosby, Stills & Nash's 'Wooden Ships' with `Cat Scratch Fever.' "It is all part of a storyline. Some- times, I'll use poetry in the middle. Sometimes I'll use spoken word," he acknowledges. "Sometimes. I'll do a set of one artist. It's all part of a large portrait I'm trying to paint on the air." The raps are not nightly affairs. "If I don't go into some outrageous rap, then listeners think there's something wrong. 411.1 Grover Washington Jr.: Reaching out to find his inner self. Discovery Bows 1st 2 Digital LPs LOS ANGELES - Discovery Rec- ords has launched its first two digital LPs, the "Bob Florence Band At Concerts By The Sea" and Russ Garcia's "Variations For Flugel- horn, String Quartet, Bass And Drums." The LPs retail for $15.98 and use the Sony digital system. A third digital project involves drummer Shelly Manne and associ- ates playing classical themes. Discovery owner Albert Marx has also cut a new Howard Roberts LP in conventional analog form. The lo- cal independent is also releasing three new titles from the Musicraft catalog which it handles on a seven - year lease basis. They are by Boyd Rayburn, Sarah Vaughan and stride pianist Herman Chitteson. Marx was a &r vice president at Musicraft when these sides were originally cut in the 1940s. The court presently owns the rights to the Mu- sicraft catalog which are adminis- tered by Oliver Savin. Already out on Musicraft are titles by Artie Shaw. Teddy Wilson and Georgie Auld with Dizzy Gillespie. In order to spread its reach, Marx says the label is now dealing direct with select jazz retailers around the country in areas where independent distribution is not available. Among these outlets are Music Peddlars in Troy, Mich., outside Detroit and the Music Plus chain here. In addition, the label is providing hand delivery to the Tower chain now that Record Merchandising is in the throes of folding. With co -owner Dennis Smith now departed, Marx has Fred Norse - worthy handling sales and promo- tion. There are 45 LPs in the Discov- ery and associate label Trend catalogs. Gillespie Will Play Atlantic City Club ATLANTIC CITY, N.J. - Bally's Park Place is rapidly developing its Billy's Pub as this resort's premier jazz club. Percussionist Mongo Santamaria holds the spotlight at the hotel ca- sino's jazz room through Wednes- day (19) followed by Dizzy Gil- lespie. Following will be Hugh Masekela from April I -May 14, then pianist Freddie Cole from May 15 -June 11. Plan is to keep the jazz beat all sum- mer long with hopes of capturing the resort's big summer disco crowd now that the disco beat is not as over- powering. Resorts International Casino Ho- tel has played such greats as Teddy Wilson and Red Norvo in its lounges, but has no steady diet of jazz as that being dished out at Park Place. Jazz Saxist Aims To Be Dr. Washington LOS ANGELES -Soon it will be Dr. Grover Washington Jr. The Elektra saxophonist is attending Temple Univ. in Philadelphia three days a week, studying composition, oral harmony and theory. "The more I play the more I real- ize I don't know," Washington ex- plains, "so I'm just going back to school to refresh myself. I want to be able to do different things -write for a picture or television show- things that mean something." Washington acknowledges that after a number of years, some of the meaning had gone out of the record - and -tour routine. "There had to be more variety," he says. "There are a lot more sides to me than that." The instrumentalist has already By PAUL GREIN made strides in branching out into new creative areas. While Creed Taylor produced all eight of his Kudu albums -from "Inner City Blues" to "Live At The Bijou" - Washington has personally pro- duced his last three: "Reed Seed" and the new "Skylarkin' " on Mo- town and last year's "Paradise" on Elektra /Asylum. "Creed was a master of record- ing," Washington says, "but I always felt I could get a little more personal with the music. Creed knew how to record, but as far as telling some- body they played too many notes in a sax solo, I'd never do that." Washington says he has complete creative control over his albums now, but he didn't at the time of 86 -Piece Orchestra In L.A. Impressive LOS ANGELES -The Orchestra is starting to make sense. This 86- piece blending of pop, jazz and clas- sically trained players is striving in its premiere season to allow innova- tive musical forces to have their say. Thus far during the Orchestra's first three concerts the results have been lacklustre. This seems to have changed with Tuesday's (11) fourth concert. For the Orchestra performed a program of varigated compositions by composers Rob McConnell, Al- lyn Ferguson and Joe Roccisano which accurately married the jazz and pop fields. Canadian McConnell's commis- sioned work. "Hello From The North," with the Orchestra's cofoun- der Allyn Ferguson conducting, had a happy lilt, a sweeping feeling which allowed for excellent solos by Bud Shank. Bill Perkins and Bill Watrous. Ferguson's own piece. "Diver- timento For Strings, Woodwinds And Percussión," exulted the strings in a romantic fashion, with an un- derlying suspenseful mood weaving through the composition. Joe Roccisano's "Synthesis For Orchestra" featured tenor man Pete Christlieb blowing blues lines over and above the jab and sock feeling Storyvilles Issued NEW YORK -The Moss Music Group is adding eight new releases to its line of Storyville jazz albums. This brings the catalog of releases to 17 since the company took over U.S. distribution of the Swedish So- net label's company last year. of the piece. With cofounder Jack Elliott handling the baton, the brass and reeds blazed away and the three -movement piece contained contrasting moody and relaxing pas- sages in addition to some space age linear lines. It was an excellent com- position for this aggregation which was able to explore the breadth of colors available to its basses and celli. Sarah Vaughan and her trio, working with the Orchestra rounded out the second half. Oscar Peterson was originally announced as the guest for this concert. Sarah wound up doing it. Unfortunately there was no creative effort to match her unique vocal abilities with the power and sweep of the Orchestra. Instead, she ran through her normal concert gig, which by itself is won- derful, but having this opportunity to work with a new orchestra, the planners blew a great opportunity. Sarah was in superb voice for her 12 tunes, all familiar to her followers and her scatting on a number of the works, lent an authentic touch of jazz singing to the program. The ar- tistic highlights: two songs she can call her own: "Feelings" and "Send In The Clowns." Both received well deserved standing ovations. Sarah's wide vocal range did won- ders to the words she caressed on such titles as "Easy Livin ." "I Got It Bad," "I Remember April," "Em- brace Me." "Our Love Is Here To Stay" and "Someone To Watch Over Me," the last three from a George Gershwin medley. But we have heard these ditties by her before. A new song in a new set - ting would have been appropriate. ELIOT TIEGEL Irakere Seeks Crossover Continued from page 3 Lundvall, who has been the inspi- rational force behind CBS' cultural links with Cuba through the signing of Irakere and the presentation of the three -day Havana Jam concert series last March featuring U.S. and Cuban jazz and rock players, admits he was "knocked out" when Irakere won the Latin Grammy. The reason? The Cubans were up against strong competition from the Fania All Stars. And it also meant that people had listened to the record and were influenced by the band's blending of cultural forces. Notes Lundvall: "Winning the Grammy is a nice reason to continue our association with Irakere because this is such a time consuming thing." This last comment refers to the time delays in dealing with the Cuban government. You just don't pick up the phone and get an immediate an- swer. Dealing with Castro's government also has its troubling side here in the U.S. An anti -Castro group calling it- self Omega 7 and operating out of Union City, N.J., has been called the "number one terrorist group in the U.S. by the FBI," Lundvall admits. This group has set several bombs off in New York to protest visiting Cu- ban musicians and is credited with killing one man. "It's a little fright- ening," Lundvall acknowledges, adding that no one at CBS ha. been harmed or threatened because of its association with Irakere. "Mister Magic" and "Feels So Good," his back -to -back 1975 al- bums which went top 10 pop. Yet he adds he still enjoys those LPs. "In spite of all the rigidity," he says, "the music is still vibrant. It comes down to the caliber of the players." Another creative area in which Washington is playing a more active role is writing, He has two tunes on the "Skylarkin' " album. compared with a total of six on all the albums with Taylor. "I've been getting a lot more confident in my writing," Washington explains. "I'm not afraid to voice my opinion now as far as my tunes go." In addition to his own tunes, Washington is able to tap musicians around him for material. Most of the songs on his Elektra "Paradise" LP were written by members of Locksmith, his backing group for the past three years. (Locksmith, in- cidentally, is now in L.A. cutting its own album, with Harvey Mason producing.) Washington says he had to give Motown two albums as a result of their mutual settlement: "Sky- larkin'," which jumps to number 50 in its third week on the pop chart, and a "best of ' retrospective, up- coming. What does Washington think of the whole phenomenon of jazz fu- sion? "As long as it swings some kind of way and says something different from what's been said before, I like it. It really comes down to how well the musicians can play." Since Washington is chasing his doctorate, he'll be off the road until 1981. His last tour was in the sum- mer of 1979, when he played 3,000 to 6,000 -seat halls. Washington's business affairs are taken care of by his wife Christine, in conjunction with Larry Magid and Murray Schwartz of Great East- ern Management. 30 (ounter- point Benefit For Franklin In Detroit Set By JEAN WILLIAMS LOS ANGELES -Aretha Frank- lin, the Rev. Cleophus Robinson and other artists are reportedly gear- ing up to perform at a benefit con- cert for the Rev. C.L. Franklin, Aretha's father. The benefit Monday (24) at De- troit's Cobo Hall comes nearly a year after the Rev. Franklin was shot dur- ing a robbery attempt at his home. The popular minister /recording art- ist was released from the hospital some time ago and reportedly re- mains comatized. As for the Rev. Cleophus Robin- son, he has been busy with concert tours and speaking engagements. It is believed he will become the first gospel artist to perform with a sym- phony orchestra in North Carolina when he does a special concert with the North Carolina Symphony Or- chestra April 13. Robinson is scheduled to perform to benefit Shaw Univ. Former film actor Thalmus Rashulala, director of special projects at Shaw, is coordi- nating the event. Robinson has a new LP on Savoy Records, "Oh Lord You Said So," his second for the label recorded live at his St. Louis church. He previ- ously was signed to Nashboro Rec- ords. * * * Teddy Pendergrass made one of his rare television appearances when he appeared on NBC -TV's "Pink Lady" show Friday (14). The singer performed two of his biggest hits, "Close The Door" and "Turn Out The Lights." Pink Lady, reportedly the largest selling female recording duo in the world, bowed with the new show on the heels of its first LP released in the U.S. The LP, issued last year, was the first by a Japanese act to hit the U.S. charts since 1963. * * * Quincy Jones received his star on Hollywood's "Walk Of Fame" Fri- day (14). According to Ed Eckstine, who runs Jones' office. "This is Quincy's 47th birthday and what do you get a guy who has everything? We didn't know so we decided to buy him a star -ha ha." Following the ceremony. spon- sored by the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce. Jones was to be honored at a luncheon at the Brown Derby. In his career, Jones has received five Grammys, one Oscar, one Emmy. two Golden Globe nomi- nations and numerous other honors. The first release on Jones' new Qwest Records will be George Ben- son's upcoming LP, which Jones is producing. The LP is a colabel deal and will he released with a Qwest/ Warner Bros. logo. General News Siegel Estate Suing His Ex- Partners By JOHN SIPPEL LOS ANGELES -The estate of the late Sheldon Harold Siegel seeks $49,000 in loan repayments, con - pensatory damages in excess of $15,000 and 20% of the shares of Merrill Enterprises Ltd. and Mush- room Records stock in a Superior Court pleading here. Ernest E. Johnson, administrator of the estate of the late vice president and general manager of Mushroom Records, who died in January 1979, claims Siegel received $57.187 in 1978 in compensation as opposed to $166,000 in 1977. He deferred salary because he was allegedly expecting to gain ownership of 20% of the shares in the two firms. Defendants include: Mushroom Records Inc. of the U.S. and Can- ada, Hunter Vogel Investment Ltd., Inkycap Holdings Inc., Chantrelle Holdings, Cloverdale Paint & Chemicals Ltd., Merrill Enterprises and Richard Hunter Vogel and Wal- ter Manson Vogel, the latter presi- dent of Mushroom. The pleading claims the corporate defendants are jointly owned by the Vogels. According to the filing, Hunter Vogel Investments Ltd., was to sell its shares in Mushroom, one -third of outstanding stock, for $150,000 with Siegel to buy 60% or 20% of the total shares while Inkycap and Chantrelle each purchased 20 %. It is further claimed Siegel was to acquire 60% of Merrill Enterprises Ltd. held by Hunter Vogel Investments with Clo- verdale Investments to obtain the re- maining 40% for the collective sale price of $150,000. As part of the agreement, Mush- room Records of Canada was to de- clare a $465.416.85 dividend, pay- able to Merrill Enterprises, which was to go to its shareholders. Siegel was to receive an annual base salary of $100,000, plus bonuses and com- missions, a car and its operational expenses and full expense account. Siegel is still owed $28,000 he per- sonally advanced to the firms a year prior to his death and $21,000 he paid attorneys for the defendants as partial consideration for the acquisi- tion of Mushroom shares, the suit contends. The court is asked to grant an ac- counting. Richard Hunter and Wal- ter Manson Vogel are accused of mismanagement and waste in con- duct of the record labels. Stix Hooper Contest MEMPHIS -The first Stix Hoo- per Drum Competition took place March I, sponsored by WHRK -FM, MCA Records and the Peaches stores. Hooper, drummer for the Crusad- ers, judged the competition of 15 semi -finalists, each of whom had three minutes to display his percus- sive techniques. The first prize winner received a complete Pearl drum set and a trophy. Second prize winner re- ceived a set of Pearl congas and all winners received a complete Cru- saders catalog as well as Stix's first solo effort, "The World Within." Conserving Energy WYOMING, Pa. -Radio Shack here is conserving energy by install- ing a geothermal heating pump, which heats through mine water. Mine water, stored about 300 feet below ground, is maintained at a constant temperature of 55 degrees by the earth's natural heat. PALLADIUM BENEFIT -Max Gail from television's "Barney Miller" and Co- lumbia artist Cheryl Lynn hold the Rossi Fund's poster child, Tanya Arrieta, at a benefit for charitable organization at the Hollywood Palladium. The Rossi Fund cares for children with cancer. Keyboard Ace Lewis Cuts LP For FM Programming By JEAN LOS ANGELES -"I took time out to study and find out what's happen- ing musically. I got a chance to talk to people in the street who told me they want records they can dance and listen to in one package. So I did an LP for FM programming," says Webster Lewis. a multi- faceted key - boardist, of his latest Epic LP "8 For The '80s." Webster, who has a masters de- gree in musical composition from the New England Conservatory, pulled together some of the nation's stellar musicians including Herbie Hancock. Wah Wah Watson. Paul Jackson Jr., James Gadson, Sheila Escovedo and Nathaniel Watts. Also WILLIAMS featured on the LP is singer /com- poser D.J. Rogers. The musician admits that "8 For The '80s" is his most commercial ef- fort Iodate. It's his third for Epic. He credits its commerciality to taking time off to determine just what the public wants, without compromising his own musicianship. Webster also has moved into out- side production and he feels strongly about what's happening to the crea- tive side of the music industry. He notes that he will produce only cer- tain types of acts. "If it's a group, I want it to be self- contained, capable of putting strong vocals to equally strong lyrics and music." PREFERS TO BE `UNSTRUCTURED' Keepnews Out But In At Fantasy Label LOS ANGELES -Although Or- rin Keepnews has resigned from Fantasy Records, the veteran a &r man will remain at the label for at least six months working on twofer LPs among other things. Fantasy, according to Phil Jones, the marketing vice president. has no plans for replacing Keepnews, and since he will still be around, Jones sees his resignation affecting the jazz operation "very little." As an independent producer, Keepnews will continue working with Fantasy artists. He is in New York producing McCoy Tyner and talking to book publishers about a title he plans to write. Keepnews points out that al- though he will be doing independ- ent production, he has no plans to form his own company. "I'm taking a wait and see atti- tude. The thing is that I want to be unstructured for awhile," he says. "Since I had heart surgery last year, 1 have been extremely healthy and find that I want to do some other things. The less time I spend in the studio the more time I spent behind a desk. "I want to stay loose. I'm letting a number of people whom I couldn't do things with before, know that I now can." As for his book, "I have already talked with a couple of publishers. I've been wanting to write about my 25 years in the music business." Keepnews is pleased with the tim- ing of his resignation "because with things the way they are now in the music industry. when you hear that someone has resigned, it's immedi- ately thought of in another way. "I have enjoyed working at Fan- tasy and will continue my relation- ship with the company, only now I'm in an unstructured situation." 38 C lossico I CBS &DG PLAN Movie Music As Sales Gooser By ALAN PENCHANSKY CHICAGO -Special album re- leases which target the moviegoer as customer and not the classical buff are being brought out by CBS Rec- ords and Deutsche Grammophon. The prominent use of classical music in major motion pictures today is viewed by both labels as a means to boost classical album sales. "Great Film Classics" is the new DG Privilege release listing at $6.98 containing classical pieces used in seven major films of the last decade. The headlining selection is as one might guess, a performance of the music that actress Bo Derek and the picture "10" have made a household word -"Bolero" by Ravel. Also contained in the new newly packaged LP are the classical selec- tions used in "Elvira Madigan," "A Clockwork Orange," "2001," "For- bidden Games," "Sunday Bloody Sunday" and "Death In Venice." The record also marks the first ap- pearance of recordings by Herbert Von Karajan in the Deutsche Grammophon mid -price series. According to Jim Lewis, vice pres- ident of marketing at PolyGram Classics, there will be heavy rack promotion, with posters and radio spots in the marketing plan. Lewis, who recently moved to PolyGram from Atlantic Records, believes that further use of classical music in films will be encouraged by the success of "10." Demand for recordings of "Also Sprach Zarathustra" soared after the piece was used in Stanley Kubrick's sci -fi smash "2001." A popularity for Mozart's Piano Concerto No. 21- the slow movement -was created by the film "Elvira Madigan." How- ever, it's believed by many dealers PHILLY DIGITAL -Philadelphia Orchestra conductor Eugene Ormandy listens to playback of a digital recording of Saint -Saens' "Organ" Symphony with Telarc Records producer Robert Woods. Tomato Introducing Series Of Soundstream Digital LPs By IRV LICHTMAN NEW YORK -Key Eggers' To- mato Records will introduce its line of Soundstream digital records within 45 days. The series, listing at $12.98 for single albums, will kick off with John Cage's "Three Constructions For Percussion" and two works for vocal and percussion featuring Jay Clayton. Also due for release is a three -LP set, listing at $29.98. of the Bach Partitas with Joao Carlos Mar- tin, who will also appear on two Bach digitals set for summer and fall release, "Goldberg Variations" and "Well- Tempered Clavier." The Bach sets are part of a series of works by the composer and Cho- pin which will appear in digital form. The Chopin project will start with a three -LP set of his Nocturnes in the fall. The label is also marketing a num- ber of non -digital albums over the next two weeks. They include the first five albums in a series of 13 of the complete Beethoven sonatas with Friedrich Gulda. The other packages include Philip Glass' "Dance 1 & 3." In addition, Tomato will release Glass works originally released on the composer's Chatham Square label. Tomato's Glass work, the four -LP "Einstein On The Beach," has re- portedly sold 30,000 copies since its release last year. according to Eg- gers. Classical Notes A survey of music by American composer Amy Beach will be broadcast by New York's WNCN- FM in May. Beach is the topic of four programs in David Dubal's series "For The Love Of Mu- sic," which airs Fridays at 2 p.m. Dubal's guest for the programs will be Patricia Williard, Moss Music Group publicist and an authority on the life and works of Beach, a New Englander who died in 1944. A recording of Beach's Piano Trio, one of her last compositions, appears in the new "Chamber Music By Women Composers" antho- logy issued by Vox. Deutsche Grammophon now confirms it will go digital in 1980. According to an official at the label, the first release -Mozart's "Magic Flute" -is due in September. Reportedly, a string of digital releases will then commence. Also look for recordings with Karajan and the Berlin Philharmonic to begin appearing in the DG mid -price Privilege line. Brahms and Beetho- ven symphony cycles recently have been re- corded by the famed conductor. Now DG is ready to release the older Karajan stereo ver- sions of these works -which some critics pre - fer-at $6.98. ALAN PENCHANSKY that the "Bolero" run is the biggest of them all. Several baroque compositions can be heard in the soundtrack to the film "Kramer Vs. Kramer," another of the boxoffice giants. This has led to the new release from CBS Master- works, which is marketing the record under an exclusive agreement with Columbia Pictures, distributor of "Kramer Vs. Kramer." "We are tieing in with this motion picture on a worldwide basis," ex- plains CBS Masterworks executive Peter Munves. "We have the rights to this album for the world." "Great CBS Masterworks Record- ings Of Baroque Favorites Featured In Kramer Vs. Kramer" is the al- bum's title. It opens with a brief snippet of the actual film sound- track, an arrangement of Vivaldi. For the remainder of the album, Masterworks catalog performances were used, and new recordings, with the English Chamber Orchestra un- der conductor Raymond Leppard. were produced. Because "Kramer vs. Kramer" uses only baroque music, the record is -in effect -the soundtrack album to the picture, says Munves. The al- bum cover will be the same as the poster used to advertise the film. "No record company can afford the kind of exposure that is coming from that type of film," Munves ex- plains. Works that are heard in "Kramer Vs. Kramer" are Vivaldi's C Major Mandolin Concerto, Purcell's So- nata For Trumpet And Strings in D Major, and Purcell's Suite "The Gordian Knot Untied." It's felt that the direction in mo- tion picture industry musical tastes may have long -range impact. Says PolyGram's Lewis: "I'm in contact with a lot of people doing musical film scores. There's a tend- ency towards greater orchestration and less electronics today. "I just see more and more movies using classically oriented music." Munves is enthusiastic about the ability to promote beyond the con- fines of the strict classical market. "You can't promote to where the market is but to where it isn't," he in- sists. "There must be at least 10 mov- ies in the 50 top grossing films today that use classical music." Oct. 23 For L.A. Disco New Light & Sound System At $6,000 Making Its Bow PITTSBURGH -After a full year of research, an area audio and video retailer is offering a low cost light and sound for clubs. Tasso Spanos, president of the Opus audio outlets, says his $6,000 system includes the lights separately for $3,000. He also claims that a quality light show at that price is a breakthrough. Simplicity is the key to Spanos' Opus One Dance Machine. Instead of the many wires that run individ- ually to each light in other systems, Spanos' system has a single wire. That wire connects to á star with lights, strobes and a spinner. The star is 11 feet wide with six arms and offers 16 different patterns. The result, Spanos says, is a sys- tem that's easily operated and easily installed. He pitches it as a disco in a day, since that's the installation time required. "Normally it would take two men one week to install a system," he says. "Or, with a bad electrician, it would take two weeks." Spanos says that business has been good even though his major marketing push hasn't yet gotten un- derway. He'll be relying heavily on past clients who have purchased Ad- vent Video Beam television systems from his two stores. "Disco will be with us for a long time," Spanos says. "Even if it's not under that name, there will be music played, and it will be played under lights on a system that's better than the ones people have at home. People will continue to go out. They're not going to hide." The break usually comes with a quality single or LP release. Irma Thomas has had moderate success since the late 1950s but never quite made it. She is back this time on RCS Records with an LP titled "Safe With Me," which is also the lead cut. She sings with a gutsy feeling that has a fine combination of funk, gospel and r&b. Her renditions of "What's The Matter Baty" and "Sugar Pie Honey Bunch" give new vitality to these classics. "Take It Where You Find It" is haunting and melodic and is another potential moer. The tracks, material and the artist need reworking, remixing and polish. However, the talent is cer- tainly there, and this woman has paid ha dues. The first Choice could probably recite the al- phabet and still be a deejaÿ s favorite. Its new LP from Gold Mind is much more complex and once again rewarding as Debbie Martin, Ro- chelle Fleming and Annette Guest combine for fine harmony. They are backed by the Don Renaldo Strings and such top musicians as Ron Kersey, Larry Washington, George Bussey, Norman Har- ris and Bob Eli to name a few. The LP titled "Breakaway" is the current 12 inch 33% r.p.m. disco disk which is starting to show action in the clubs. Other highlights include "Pressure Point," "Can't Take It With You" (mixer by New York deejay Tae Scott), and "A Happy Love Af- fair" and "I Can Show You." American Gypsy is a Dutch r &b /rock group that has released its European hit "rill O.K., You're O.K." on Importe /12 Records. Available on a 12 -inch 33% r.p.m. the group has ex- tended its tune to 10:49 as remixed bi Raul of New York, New York. The music is harsh, synthesized and well ar- ranged. The spectrum of the group's appeal should be broad as it will appeal to Loth rock and disco enthusiasts. Though the disk is some- what lengthy, an exciting and smooth flow is maintained with enough variations in arrange- ment to keep interest sustained. Judy Cheeks has returned with a driving 12- inch 33% r.p.m. produced and arranged by Thor Baldursson. After a previously disappointing LP, Cheeks' latest effort is a step beyond where "Mellow Lovin' " left off. Intense instrumenta- tion as well as vocalization reach out on the up- lifting track which runs for 5:20. Titled "Don't Wanna Love You Again" and mixed by Juergen Koppers, it is available on Dream Records. Atco Records has new wave /rock atist Gary Numan's LP release titled the "Pleasure Prin- ciple." The music is a cross between '(raftwerk and Jean Michael Jarre. The cuts are heavily synthesized but well- crafted and con;ise. In France, Disco Alive, Doing Well PARIS -People are dancing in France. Figures from the local disco- theque syndicate show an average national weekly attendance of more than seven million for clubs, with the average disco pulling in 1,500- 2,000 customers each week. And this despite growing prej- udices, particularly among the po- lice, backed by local authorities, that discos somehow incite violence. Disco owners through their syndi- cate claim this is "absurd," that vio- lence never, or only very rarely breaks out in the discos themselves, but generally takes place outside. Not enough is done, says the syndi- cate, to show that disco fans are bas- ically responsible young people anx- ious to keep out of trouble. 60 Disco Forum Report Hot Seaters Criticize Top 40 And Label Execs By JEAN WILLIAMS Top 40 radio and record com- panies carne under fire at the Hot Seat session of the Disco Forum when Bill Wardlow the Forum direc- tor and session moderator charged the two with orchestrating disco's backlash. He further blasted some label heads for being "20 years be- hind the times." The hypocrisy is that radio is programming r &b /disco and rock/ disco," he said. He apologized to the audience (50% club owners) for what he called watering down the name disco to Dance Music Forum, vowing that the next conference will be called International Disco Forum VIII. Wardlow's statement set the tone for the more than two -hour session. Most of the 19 panelists re- iterated Wardlow's statement. "We will not be intimidated by la- bels nor by radio for its lack of pro- gramming knowledge. Disco will be the catalyst for carrying r &b across to pop in the '80s," he claimed. Wardlow angrily challenged record companies to enlarge the budgets of r &b departments and suggested they bring on disco people to work closely with r &b reps. He added that disco saw la- bels through a lean period. He advised that disco records will be charted with or without Top 40 airplay. He cited as an example for this statement Gloria Gaynor's "Never Can Say Goodbye," which was charted based on sales, which he said forced Top 40 radio to play the disk. Sitting on the panel were George Borden, Jane Brinton, Jim Bur- gess, Ray Caviano, Mel Cheren, Linda Emon, Dino Fekaris, Scott Forbes, Steve Gold, Tom Hayden, Wayne Johnson, A.J. Miller, Wayne Rosso, Dick Sheppard, Mark Simon, Arnie Smith, Judy Weinstein, Frankie Crocker and Mark Kreiner. Maintained Steve Gold: You are not going to get the kind of cooper- ation you would get if you were white rock'n'roll; you're in the back of the bus now and you now know what it's about." He was speaking of dollars allocated by labels for r &b and disco acts versus monies spent on rock'n'roll artists. Some of the panelists had differ- ent philosophies and long range goals of disco, as Linda Emon said: "Roller disco is new but it's not just dancing, it's a sport and we're gear- ing up for the 1988 olympics." PATRICE RUSHEN DAN HARTMAN LOLEATTA HOLLOWAY Studio One, Los Angeles The first night of the Forum's entertainment got off to a slow start. Those attending had to wait over two hours until preparations were fi- nalized. Fault seems to lie with Studio One which was not fully prepared for the evening's entertainment and with Sounds Unlimited, the company hired to handle the sound reinforce- ment for all the acts. Finally, the opening act, Patrice Rushen of Elektra Records appeared on stage to perform her chart hit "Haven't You Heard." The crowd was disappointed with the fact that the artist lip- synched over the record. Not only did this not work but her exciting open- ing number was followed by a quiet ballad for which the audience was not ready, did not ap- preciate. Presumably Rushen is in preparation for a live act, and perhaps should have held off performing until she was completely ready. She does exude personality on the stage and was a pleasure to see, but for a first appearance, her performance did not go well with forum regis- trants. Had she performed an uptempo song from her LP "Pizzazz," instead of the ballad, the crowd reaction might have been more encour- aging. For the last several weeks Dan Hartman and Loleatta Holloway have held the number one spot on the disco charts with "Vertigo /Relight My Fire." They were smart in providing the au- dience with an extended 15 minute version of this hit. Hartman came out, after the "Vertigo" introduction to a fog enshrouded stage, playing the piano. As this instrumental beginning led into the vocals of "Relight My Fire" the sound was almost lost due to the audience's cheers. Hartman is becoming a good stage performer al- though his presence in the beginning of this act still seemed a bit stilted. He does not seem as enthusiastic as his music. However, as the song progressed, he became more involved and was jumping as much on the stage as was the au- dience on the floor. However, the highlight cer- tainly had to be when Loleatta Holloway started her vocals. To say the crowd went wild is an un- Forum Entertainment derstatement. As a performer, Holloway is a dy- namo with a voice that belts out lyrics with an exciting gospel -like feeling. Both performers did some improvisation midway through the song. As a duet they work well together and additional recordings by the two would certainly be wel- come. * * * WAR Bonnie Pointer The group WAR was an unexpected surprise for those at the Forum and was very welcome. Of their nine piece band, six of the members go back to the group's beginning in 1969. The opening number The World Is A Ghetto" with a clarinet solo carrying the melody, led into four other instrumental solos. All the members of the group had their chance to show their respective expertise. Unfortunately, partway through the performance, two of the mikes went dead. How- ever, the group continued without any apparent concern. Other songs included in their 45 -min- ute appearance were "Don't Take It Away," their latest single "Sunny Day," "Spill The Wine" and of course the infamous "Slipping Into Dark- ness." During this last number the harmonica solo by Lee Oscar was one of the highlights of the entire concert. "Cisco Kid" began with a long drum introduction followed by guitar and keyboard melody. Other outstanding hits in- cluded "Gypsy Man" which began with a de- lightful harmonica and clavinet introduction fol- lowed by a long and winding electric keyboard. The rise and fall in the tempo of this song capti- vated the audience. Compliments to Lonnie Jor- dan on keyboards who also provided some of the lead vocals. His amazing strength in this per- formance was certainly felt by the crowd. Instru- mental guitarist Howard Scott along with Harold Brown on drums, Tweed Smith vocalist, Lou Careb on guitar, Ronnie Hammond on drums, Pat Russo on tenor sax and Poppa D on congas and bongos, rounded out this proficient group. The final number "Why Can't We Be Friends," had the entire audience singing along and gave affirmation to this group's durability. Two of the hottest songs out this year have been performed by Bonnie Pointer. They are "Heaven Must Have Sent You" and her latest hit "I Can't Help Myself," (Sugar Pie). The seven piece band that backed her was obviously not strong enough to give the impact that her studio performances do. Even at the last Forum, with the addition of strings, the dynamic personality of Pointer seemed to be lost without her original tracks. Not only did her ballads fail to come across, but there were audio feedback problems during her 45- minute performance which in- cluded "Free Me From My Freedom," "Come See About Me," "More and More," "Deep Inside My Soul," "Sugar Pie," "Nowhere to Run" and "Heaven Must Have Sent You." Pointer is an en- tertainer with a tremendous amount of energy, and is a favorite among the deejays. However, she should think twice before attempting to do a live performance with a band unless she is fully prepared. Other performers that decided to use prerecorded tapes were better received though Pointer did not leave the stage without appre- ciative ovations. * * * DEBBIE JACOBS PEACHES & HERB The third night of Forum entertainment was very well received with both groups giving high level performances. Debbie Jacobs began her selections with "Undercover Lover," then went into "High On Your Love" (Paul Sabu on guitar), "Ain't The Way," "Don't You Want My Love," "You Can Never Forget A Friend," and a new re- mix of "Hotter Than Hot." Jacobs used prere- corded tapes which worked well for her that eve- ning . Her stage presence was invigorating, and she related well to the crowd. For the first time there was no problem with the sound system. Many consider this evening one of Debbie's fin- est performances, with you "Don't You Want My Love" completely breaking up the crowd into nonstop applause. Peaches and Herb have been around for some time and their expertise on the stage was apparent throughout the evening. Whatever they sang worked well. Their 60- minute program included "We've Got Love," "How About Some Love" (from their latest album), "Love Lift," "I Pledge My Love," (their latest single) "Reu- nited" (their number one hit) and "Shake Your Groove Thing" another number one hit. Their six piece band included two keyboards, bongos, rhythm and bass guitar and drums. The group has tight coordination and gave a tremendous performance backing up Peaches & Herb. All the songs were spirited and well coordinated. Unfor- tunately part of the sound went out during "I Pledge My Love." * * * ANN -MARGRET PAUL SABU Ann -Margret first electrified Forum attendees at Disco Vi last summer at New York's Roseland. Her brief one song performance then gave her a recording contract and a firm start in the disco market. This time around, this seasoned per- former was better prepared for her audience. Her songs included "Rain Satin," with backup dancers for added excitement, "Love Rush," "Midnight Message" and "Dancing Man." Ann - Margret is no newcomer to performing on the stage. Her background in this field was more than evident with a stage presence that high- lighted the week's entertainment. She is able to cross from the field of cabaret entertainment to disco performer with ease. Paul Sabu came on stage with his entire band including Rick Bozo on bass, Stephen Presley on keyboards, Dan Holmes on percussion and Sabu, playing all guitars. The group's selections. included "Shaking Loose," "I Want To Feel In My Heart," "Wet and Wild," their current 12 inch "We're Gonna Rock," "Street Heart," "Rock Me Slowly" and the new single from their LP "For Lovers Only." The overall effect pleased the audience, however, the emphasis seemed to be too rock oriented. I think those in attendance would have preferred more emphasis on a disco beat and a slightly shorter concert. Overall the group is extremely talented. Credit must be given to Bob Small and Harvey Bolgla for their coordination of all the evening's events. This was one of the smoothest running entertain- ment events to be staged during Billboard's Disco Forums. Except for some apparent prob- lems from the sound cmpany and a delay in opening, all the acts were on time. It is hoped that in future planning of the entertainment more groups such as WAR to which the deejays and those attending the convention are not ex- posed, will be utilized. www.americanradiohistory.com

68 International Fresh Figures Affirm German Sales Decline HAMBURG- Statistical confir- mation of sluggish sales in Germany last year comes in new data released by the country's industry group, Bundesverband der Phonographis- chen Wirtschaft. Figures show that 183.4 million records and tapes were sold during 1979, a three percent drop against the previous year's figure of 188.3 million records and tapes. Only unit sales information is available at present -Deutsch Mark figures will follow later -but despite the three percent slump, market value is expected to exceed one bil- lion DM for the second successive year. Statistical breakdown of the data indicates that singles gained 3% dur- ing the year in review, with 47.8 mil- lion sold; full -price albums gained 10% with 61.9 million units sold; and budget price LPs declined a dra- matic 18% to 36.3 million units, a downturn largely attributed to the effects of home taping. Combining full -price and budget albums yields a dip of 2% (at 98.2 million units) compared to the pre- vious 12 months. Declines are also evident when the musicassette figures are broken out, with full -price tapes off by 13% (14.2 million sold) and budget tapes off by 7% (21.5 million). Double - play cassettes also slumped, by 15% to 1.7 million units. Overall, prerecorded cassettes to- talled 37.4 million units, a drop of 10% against the previous year. Further breakdown of the figures show total sales of records and tapes in the pop music category to be 169.4 million units, down by 3% compared to 1978. The classical market for disks and tapes actually increased against the previous 12 months, at 14 million units. This includes a 14% jump in sales of budget -price tapes, at 800,000 units. BBC ORCHESTRAS Sponsors Could Save Musicians From Axe By PETER JONES LONDON -There's a reasonable chance that outside private sponsor- ship will help save at least one of the five British Broadcasting Corp. or- chestras currently threatened with the axe under the corporation's planned $270 million economy cuts (Billboard, March 15, 1980). This optimistic prospect for at least the Scottish Symphony Orches- tra has emerged from a series of still - continuing talks between BBC offi- cials and leading musicians and mu- sic societies. Overall, 172 musicians are af- fected by the cutbacks, but concern is strongest for the Scottish Sym- phony. Newspapers, magazines and radio have given much space and time to protests about the orchestra's projected exit from the nation's mu- sical life, including those from such prestigious names as Peter Pears. Sir Adrian Boult, Andrew Davis and composer Peter Maxwell Davies. Sir Anthony Lewis, principal of the Royal Academy of Music was jeopardized. "It relies for many of its teaching staff on the orchestra, and all music schools are worried about the narrowing of opportunities for their students." Members of the Incorporated Society of Musicians, which repre- sents 7,000 performers, composers and teachers, are petitioning the BBC, suggesting the corporation should consider advertising on Ra- dios I and 2, or straight commercial sponsorship, to keep the orchestras going. And many in the music world fra- ternity, particularly on the classical side, cannot see why the BBC con- tinues to boost its local radio net- work, an area seen as well -covered by the independent commercial sta- tions, while slashing costs on its cul- tural activities. The Incorporated Society of Mu- sicians insists that once the orches- tras have been "destroyed," then they'll be lost for ever. BBC claims that even after the cuts, it leads the world in providing more orchestras than any other broadcasting organization are chal- lenged. And Bronze has also signed an all- female group, Girls School, with "Emer- gency" as its first 45 for the German market, where the group will tour later. tras -three in light music -left, em- ploying 379 musicians, whereas the six symphony orchestras of the Aus- tralian Broadcasting Corp. have 443 musicians on call. The Musicians Union has already asked for help from the British Pho- nographic Industry (BPI) in its fight to save the orchestras. John Morton, union secretary, is particularly incensed by the fact that the BBC announced its cutback plans with no prior consultation with the union. "We finally received a formal statement, and a meeting has at least been arranged for Wednesday (19). "It's clear that the BBC is a great propaganda organization. People are falling for its line that these or- chestras could be removed without unduly affecting the corporation's musical output. Certainly I refute al- legations that the light orchestras in- volved are dispensible because they're outmoded or old- fashioned." And the Royal Television Society is suggesting that an independent body, jointly financed by the BBC and the commercial television and radio contractors, should take over all II existing BBC orchestras in or- der to "safeguard their future." Philip Sidey, society chairman and also head of the BBC network production center in midlands, says: "An independent organization would act as an umbrella for the or- chestras and could become maybe the largest employer of musicians in the world." French TV Sets Song Promotion By HENRY KAHN PARIS -The French Third tele- vision network, which covers 18 re- gional stations, is making a major commitment this year to popularize the "chanson Francaise." It will seek out new singers, lyr- icists and composers in this musical genre. anticipating a flood of new material and talent in 1980, hailed as "French heritage" year. Each region covered by the net- -work has its own musical folklore emphasis, adding variety to the "buy French" thrust. Brittany has made a strong start, opening an academy dedicated to the chanson style; com- ing soon is a mass release of new Breton -based recordings. The Chanson francais is also being boosted by a contest organ- ized by the Societe des Auteurs, Compositeurs et Editeurs de Musi- que (SACEM) and Radio Luxembourg. The event involves a series of half - hour programs on Luxembourg when the public will be invited to nominate its favorite chanson items. Contest will be run in three sections: song of 1979, songs of the 1960 -79 period and songs from before 1960. The final top 10 will comprise three from each group, and one drawn by a special jury from another list. It's all seen as evidence of the in- dustry's drive to demonstrate that French songs can compete with U.S. and U.K. compositions, given the right exposure. A special Founda- tion of French Song was formed pre- viously, and a special festival organ- ized for this kind of music. www.americanradiohistory.com
